title: 1,800+ Student Visas Revoked at 280 Colleges; SEVIS Terminations Widespread
synopsis: Beginning in late March 2025, the Trump administration conducted a sweeping, largely unexplained mass revocation of international student visas and SEVIS status terminations. Secretary of State Rubio initially acknowledged revoking approximately 300 visas; an AP review as of April 15 found at least 1,024 students at 160 institutions affected. Inside Higher Ed's tracking database grew to over 1,800 students at 280+ colleges across 45 states and D.C. by late April. Universities reported that the federal government provided no reasons for most terminations; some students were targeted for pro-Palestine protest activity, others for minor criminal charges such as a desk-appearance ticket. The University of California system totaled 76 affected students. At least 290 students filed in 65 separate lawsuits; the administration announced April 25 it would restore all terminated SEVIS statuses pending further review, then continued targeted revocations. AI-assisted social media screening was used to identify targets.

title: Bears Ears and Grand Staircase Shrunk 90% in Utah Land Grab
synopsis: On July 13, 2026, Trump signed proclamations under the Antiquities Act reducing Bears Ears National Monument from approximately 1.36 million acres to 121,096 acres — a 91% cut — and Grand Staircase-Escalante from 1.87 million acres to 181,541 acres — a 90% cut — removing nearly 3 million combined acres of protected land. Both monuments contain ancient cliff dwellings, petroglyphs, and coal and uranium deposits coveted by industry. Trump had taken similar actions in 2017 that Biden reversed. Critics called it a giveaway to mining and energy interests over sacred Native American lands.

title: Clean Power Plan Successor Rules Proposed for Full Repeal
synopsis: On June 11, 2025, EPA Administrator Zeldin proposed repealing all greenhouse gas emission standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants under Section 111 of the Clean Air Act, including the Biden-era 'Clean Power Plan 2.0' finalized in May 2024. The proposal argued that GHG emissions from power plants 'do not contribute significantly to dangerous air pollution,' a reversal of decades of EPA scientific findings. EPA's own regulatory impact analysis projected $19 billion in compliance cost savings from 2026–2047 under 3% discount rates, but did not calculate the climate damage costs. The EPA also proposed repealing Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS) amendments that were forcing coal plant shutdowns.

title: Coal Plant Lifeline: DOE Emergency Orders Keep Dying Plants Online
synopsis: Beginning May 23, 2025, Energy Secretary Chris Wright invoked emergency authority under Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act to force the J.H. Campbell coal plant in Michigan — which was scheduled to permanently close — to remain operational, over the objections of both the grid operator and the plant's owner, Consumers Energy. The plant had been in a multi-year retirement process approved in 2022. CNN reported the move would cost Midwest ratepayers in 15 states tens of millions of dollars. The DOE subsequently issued additional emergency coal orders for plants in Indiana, Washington state, Colorado (Craig Station, December 30, 2025), and others. The regional grid operator MISO said it had not requested the Michigan extension.

title: Endangered Species Act 'Harm' Definition Rescinded, Opening Habitats
synopsis: On July 10–11, 2026, the Interior and Commerce Departments finalized a rule rescinding the regulatory definition of 'harm' under the Endangered Species Act (ESA), effective September 14, 2026. For 50 years, 'harm' had included habitat modification or degradation that kills or injures wildlife by impairing essential behaviors — a protection upheld by the Supreme Court in 1995. The new rule means oil drilling, mining, logging, and development can proceed in critical habitats so long as animals are not directly killed. A separate rule finalized July 17, 2026 required economic impact analyses when designating critical habitat. CNN called it 'reversing 50 years of environmental law.' Environmentalists warned it could drive multiple species toward extinction.

title: Wildfire Policy Failure: Prescribed Burns Halved, Four Firefighters Dead
synopsis: In 2025, the U.S. Forest Service — having lost 16% of its workforce (5,860 staff) under DOGE cuts — reduced hazardous fuel treatment by 1.5 million acres compared to 2024, including cutting prescribed burns nearly in half from over 1.6 million acres to roughly 900,000 acres. Agriculture Secretary Rollins and Interior Secretary Burgum then ordered a sweeping 'full suppression' policy for 2026, abandoning decades of science-backed managed fire strategies. On June 27, 2026, four federal firefighters died when the Snyder Fire in Colorado overran their position. Trump created the U.S. Wildland Fire Service by secretarial order — pulling 3,900 Interior firefighters from six agencies — without congressional approval. By August 2026, millions of acres were burning across the West under unprecedented drought conditions.

title: Big Beautiful Bill Kills IRA Clean Energy Tax Credits
synopsis: On July 4, 2025, Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21), which repealed or sharply restricted nearly every clean energy tax credit enacted under the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act. The EV consumer tax credits (Sections 30D, 25E, 45W) were repealed for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025; the Residential Clean Energy Credit (solar, geothermal; Section 25D) was repealed for installations after December 31, 2025. The Joint Committee on Taxation projected the law would reduce federal clean energy expenditures by roughly $267 billion in consumer credits and over $48 billion in advanced manufacturing credits through 2033. Wind and solar projects were made ineligible for clean electricity investment and production tax credits unless entering service before January 1, 2028.

title: Title IX Reverted to 2020 Rules, Transgender Student Protections Stripped
synopsis: On January 20, 2025, Trump signed an executive order declaring only two biological sexes exist and directing all federal agencies to reinterpret sex-based statutes accordingly, explicitly rescinding 11 Biden-era Title IX guidance documents protecting LGBTQ+ students. On January 31, the Department of Education issued a Dear Colleague letter to all schools confirming immediate enforcement of the 2020 Title IX regulations — which exclude gender identity from sex discrimination protections — effective retroactively for all open investigations. On February 5, Trump signed an additional executive order directing the DOJ to enforce a ban on transgender girls and women in female school sports under Title IX, threatening federal funding cuts for noncompliance. Schools in 26 states that had already reverted under prior court orders were joined by every other U.S. institution, eliminating transgender bathroom access, pronoun policies, and harassment protections at federally funded schools nationwide.

title: USDA/RFK Dietary Guidelines Politicized; NIH Nutrition Research Gutted
synopsis: In March 2025, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins and RFK Jr. announced a 'line-by-line review' of the 2025 Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee's science report, with Kennedy pledging guidelines as short as four pages — compared to the prior 164-page document — potentially contradicting scientific consensus on saturated fats, seed oils, and red meat. The NIH's lead ultra-processed food researcher resigned in April 2025 after 21 years, citing fear of censorship. The Trump budget proposed cutting NIH nutrition research funding while also eliminating the CDC's National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion ($1.4 billion annual budget). Scientists and CSPI condemned the MAHA Commission's strategy report for including fake citations and pseudoscientific claims, while the administration canceled over $1 billion in local food funding and terminated NIH grants covering nutrition and diet-related disease research.

title: Pentagon DEI Purge: 188 Positions Abolished, Advisory Committee Disbanded
synopsis: On January 27, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14185 directing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to abolish every DEI office within the Department of Defense, including all sub-offices, programs, and initiatives. According to a Government Accountability Office report released April 17, 2025, the DOD had cut or restructured 188 DEI-related civilian and military positions since early 2024. The congressionally chartered Defense Advisory Committee on Diversity and Inclusion was disbanded, and a Pentagon task force was created in February 2025 to oversee and certify the complete elimination of DEI activity across all military branches. By March 1, 2025, the task force certified no DEI goals remained in organizational composition, academic admissions, or career fields across any branch.

title: Penn $175M Research Halted; Stanford 82 Grants Cut; Universities Targeted
synopsis: In March 2025, the Trump administration issued stop-work orders on $175 million in federally contracted research across seven schools at the University of Pennsylvania, citing the university's 2022 allowance of a transgender athlete on the women's swim team — even though Penn stated it was already complying with the new Title IX rules. The halted contracts covered research on preventing hospital infections, drug screening against viruses, quantum computing, chemical warfare defenses, and student loan programs. Stanford University reported 82 federally supported grant terminations by September 2025, totaling $41.2 million. Dozens of other research universities — including Harvard, Columbia, Penn, and institutions across 26 states — faced NIH and NSF grant terminations as the administration used research funding as political leverage in a broader campaign against universities.

title: Big Beautiful Bill Medicaid Cuts: 10 Million Lose Coverage
synopsis: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21), signed by Trump on July 4, 2025, contains approximately $840 billion in Medicaid cuts over ten years. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimated on July 21, 2025 that the law's health provisions would leave 10 million more Americans without insurance by 2034. The law's community engagement (work) requirements alone — which mandate that able-bodied, non-elderly adults prove employment, education, or community service to retain Medicaid — will reduce federal Medicaid outlays by $325.6 billion and cause 4.8 million people to lose coverage by 2034. An additional 1.3 million people with both Medicaid and Medicare would lose their Medicaid coverage. Democrats and health advocacy groups called the cuts the largest reduction to Medicaid in the program's 60-year history.

title: ACA Navigator Program Slashed 90%, Enrollment Rules Tightened
synopsis: On February 14, 2025 — the day after RFK Jr. was sworn in as HHS secretary — the Trump administration announced it would cut the ACA Navigator program from $98 million to $10 million annually, a reduction of $360 million over four years. Navigators are community-based organizations that help low-income and uninsured Americans enroll in ACA marketplace plans; in 2024 they served roughly 4.6 million people with counseling and enrollment assistance. The administration justified the cut by claiming navigators enrolled only 0.6% of marketplace selections at a cost of $1,061 per enrollment. In June 2025, CMS also finalized rules shortening the open enrollment window to end December 15 (one month earlier) and eliminating the monthly special enrollment period for those below 150% of the federal poverty line, which had been created to help the most vulnerable sign up year-round.

title: SNAP Food Stamp Cuts: 2.7 Million Lose Benefits Under OBBBA
synopsis: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act enacted on July 4, 2025 imposed the largest cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) in the program's history, reducing federal SNAP spending by over $280 billion over ten years. CBO analyses released in August 2025 found that expanded work requirements will cause 2.4 million fewer Americans to receive benefits in an average month, including parents of dependent children newly subject to work mandates for the first time. An additional 300,000 people will lose benefits beginning in 2028 when states are required to share benefit costs, with some states expected to leave the program entirely. A cap on Thrifty Food Plan updates will reduce the average monthly benefit from a projected $227 to $213 by 2034. Groups most at risk include veterans, people experiencing homelessness, and young adults aging out of foster care.

title: Medication Abortion Under Siege: FDA Review, Comstock Threat
synopsis: In May 2025, HHS Secretary RFK Jr. directed the FDA to launch a safety review of mifepristone — the first medication in a two-drug regimen used in 63% of U.S. abortions — which experts warned could lead to tighter telehealth restrictions, mandatory in-person prescriptions, or removal from pharmacy shelves. As of July 2025, 12 states had total abortion bans and nine states explicitly banned telehealth-provided medication abortion. The Trump Justice Department was also weighing a broader interpretation of the 1873 Comstock Act that could ban mailing abortion pills nationwide regardless of state law. Texas in September 2025 passed a law allowing private citizens to sue physicians, manufacturers, and distributors from outside the state who mail abortion medication into Texas — a direct attack on blue-state shield laws. Louisiana grand-juried a New York doctor in January 2025 for providing telehealth abortions to a patient in Louisiana.

title: Title X Family Planning Freeze: 879 Clinics, 834,000 Patients at Risk
synopsis: On March 31, 2025, the Trump administration froze Title X family planning funding for 16 of 86 grantees, withholding more than $65 million that had been earmarked for contraception, STI testing, and cancer screenings at clinics serving low-income and uninsured patients. All nine Planned Parenthood federation affiliates with Title X grants were affected, as were seven other nonprofit grantees. KFF estimated 879 clinics in 23 states — 24% of all Title X clinics — were impacted, and up to 834,000 people could lose access to Title X-funded care. HHS cited unspecified civil rights violations and Trump's executive order barring benefits to undocumented immigrants but refused to detail the alleged infractions. By late April 2025, dozens of clinics had begun closing. Title X serves 2.8 million clients annually across nearly 4,000 clinics, with 83% of patients having family incomes at or below 250% of the federal poverty level.

title: Drug Pricing EOs: Biden Pilot Programs Killed, MFN Order Has No Teeth
synopsis: On January 20, 2025, Trump rescinded Executive Order 14087 — Biden's 2022 order directing HHS to develop new models to lower drug costs for Medicare and Medicaid patients, including a proposed $2 monthly cap on generic drugs. While the IRA's $35 insulin cap and $2,000 annual out-of-pocket cap remained intact as statutory law, the cancellation ended three CMS Innovation Center pilot programs before they could be implemented. On May 12, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14297 directing drugmakers to align U.S. prices with the lowest prices in comparable developed nations ('most favored nation' pricing); pharma stocks rose on the announcement as analysts and legal experts questioned how it could be enforced. Congressional Research Service analysis noted the order lacked defined legal authority and could conflict with existing IRA drug negotiation provisions. No major price reductions had materialized from the MFN order by August 2025.

title: Rural Hospital Closures: 300+ at Risk from $840B Medicaid Cuts
synopsis: A June 2025 analysis by the Cecil G. Sheps Center for Health Services Research found that over 300 financially struggling rural hospitals were at heightened risk of closure, service reductions, or ending inpatient care due to the OBBBA's Medicaid cuts. Nearly half of all rural hospitals were already operating in the red before the law's enactment, and the cuts were projected to drain $1.8 billion from rural hospital net revenues with a 15% Medicaid reduction. The law included a $50 billion, five-year Rural Health Transformation Program, but Health Affairs analysis found it was not required to flow to rural hospitals, was run by CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz with broad discretion, and expired after five years while Medicaid cuts were permanent. By early 2026, rural hospitals in Nebraska, North Carolina, New Hampshire, Minnesota, Virginia, and Oklahoma were closing services, with INTEGRIS Health citing a projected $130 million loss.

title: Liberation Day: Trump's Global Tariff Shock Rattles World Markets
synopsis: On April 2, 2025, President Trump declared a national economic emergency and announced sweeping tariffs from the Rose Garden — a 34% rate on China, 20% on the European Union, 24% on Japan, and a 10% baseline on virtually all other nations, branding it 'Liberation Day.' Global markets reacted immediately: Japan's Nikkei dropped nearly 4%, Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 1.5%, and U.S. Dow futures were down 2.5% pre-market. JPMorgan analysts warned the tariffs would impose a $660 billion annual tax increase on Americans, raise CPI by 2%, and likely push the U.S. and global economies into recession in 2025 — raising their recession probability estimate from 40% to 60%. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it 'a major blow to the world economy' with 'dire' consequences for millions of people.

title: 25% Auto Tariffs Devastate Ford, GM, Stellantis: $108B in Costs
synopsis: Trump's 25% tariffs on imported vehicles took effect April 3, 2025, with 25% tariffs on auto parts set to follow by May 3. The Center for Automotive Research calculated the tariffs would increase costs for all US automakers by $107.7 billion in 2025 — $41.9 billion for Ford, GM, and Stellantis alone. Goldman Sachs estimated new vehicle prices would rise $2,000-$4,000; Cox Automotive projected a $6,000 increase for fully imported vehicles. Stellantis idled factories in Canada and Mexico making Chrysler and Jeep vehicles, laying off 900 US workers; Jaguar Land Rover suspended all US exports; Porsche halted European shipments. Analyst firm Telemetry projected upward of 2 million fewer vehicles sold annually in the US and Canada. Trump partially softened the tariffs April 29 by offering credits for domestically assembled vehicles, but core levies remained.

title: $6.6 Trillion Wiped From Markets in Historic Post-Tariff Crash
synopsis: The two trading days following Trump's Liberation Day tariff announcement — April 3 and 4, 2025 — produced the largest two-day S&P 500 market value destruction on record, surpassing even the COVID-19 crash of March 2020. The S&P 500 lost approximately $5 trillion in market cap by Reuters' count, with WSJ reporting a total of $6.6 trillion erased. The Dow Jones fell 1,679 points on April 3 alone, its biggest single-day drop since June 2020; the Nasdaq confirmed it entered a bear market, falling more than 20% from its December 2024 peak. Apple lost $315 billion in market cap in a single day — the second-largest single-stock decline on record. By the 100-day mark of Trump's second term, over $6.5 trillion had been wiped from public company valuations, making it the worst stock market start to any presidential term since Gerald Ford in 1974.

title: Tariff-Driven Grocery Inflation Hits Fastest Pace Since 2022
synopsis: By August 2025, US grocery prices had risen at their fastest monthly pace since 2022, with the food-at-home CPI component jumping 0.6% in a single month, up 2.7% year-over-year, driven in part by Trump's tariffs on imports from China, steel, aluminum, and other nations. Coffee prices surged 20.9% year-over-year as of August 2025; uncooked beef steaks rose 16.6%; apples climbed 9.6%; bananas 6.6%. Yale University's Budget Lab estimated food prices would rise 3.4% in the short run and remain 2.5% higher long-run under Trump's tariff levels. A Federal Reserve analysis found tariffs accounted for roughly 0.5 percentage points of annualized headline PCE inflation in June-August 2025 and explained 10.9% of annual PCE inflation for the 12 months ending August 2025. Trump had campaigned on a pledge to lower grocery prices.

title: Section 232 Steel and Aluminum Tariffs Doubled to 50% in June 2025
synopsis: On June 3, 2025, Trump signed a proclamation under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 doubling steel and aluminum tariffs from 25% to 50%, effective June 4 — on top of the February 2025 expansion that had already removed all country exemptions and raised aluminum tariffs to 25% globally. The 50% rate applied to all countries except the UK, which was held at 25% under the US-UK Economic Prosperity Deal. In August 2025, the Commerce Department added over 400 product codes to the tariff scope, including household appliances. By year-end 2025, US steel imports had fallen 21% compared to 2024 — from $31.6 billion to $24.8 billion — while aluminum imports fell 5% to $17.5 billion. The cumulative Section 232 tariff actions in 2025, combined with IEEPA-based universal tariffs, produced the most restrictive US trade policy since before World War II.

title: '90 Deals in 90 Days' Collapses: Only 2 Deals Reached by Deadline
synopsis: When Trump announced the 90-day tariff pause on April 9, 2025, White House trade adviser Peter Navarro boasted of '90 deals in 90 days,' and Trump himself claimed at his 100-day mark to have struck deals with '200 countries.' By the July 9 deadline, only two formal agreements had been reached — a partial framework with the United Kingdom and a preliminary deal with Vietnam. Trump then extended his own 'final' deadline to August 1, declaring 'no extensions will be granted,' only to extend it again. By July 9, 2025, CNN reported just three deals (UK, Vietnam, and China's partial 90-day tariff reduction), far short of the promised comprehensive restructuring of global trade. Foreign officials across 10 countries told Politico that negotiations were bogged down. The EU ultimately settled for a 15% tariff deal just days before August 1, with France immediately declaring it needed renegotiation.

title: EO 14168: 'Two Sexes Only' Order Rewrites Federal Law
synopsis: Executive Order 14168, 'Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government,' signed January 20, 2025, declared it official federal policy to 'recognize two sexes, male and female' defined by 'immutable biological classification' at conception. The order directed all federal agencies to apply this definition when interpreting statutes, regulations, and guidance; replace the term 'gender' with 'sex' on all federal documents; remove gender-identity fields from agency forms; and direct the attorney general to issue guidance limiting the scope of Bostock v. Clayton County to narrow hiring and promotions decisions, specifically excluding its application to Title IX and Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act. The order rescinded five prior executive orders including EOs 13988, 14004, 14020, 14021, and 14075, dissolved the White House Gender Policy Council, and required a proposed bill to codify the definitions within 30 days. It applied to passports, visas, federal employee records, prison housing, and all federally funded entities including contractors, affecting an estimated 314,000 LGBTQ federal employees and contractors.
